report:
北京时间 2026-11-23 技术雷达

今天最重要变化：VLA 的优化焦点从“单模型更强”转向“把推理当作可调度、可中断、可压缩的运行时负载”。多客户端推理测量、事件触发中断、世界模型一步蒸馏、3D token 剪枝与触觉前向执行同日出现，指向同一个方向：在没有充分基准前，先建立 VLA 运行时的分层控制与资源账本。

---

**1. VLA 多客户端推理的系统测量**
《Analysis of Multi-Client Inference Techniques for Vision-Language-Action Models》，2026-11-23，arXiv cs.RO，https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26944

它试图解决旧问题：VLA serving 因 action chunking 导致 GPU 在两次推理间长期空闲，作者报告空闲时间 >80% 总任务时间；单次推理也远未打满，SM throughput 21–27%，其中 action expert（AE）最低，仅约 5–19%。核心机制不是新模型，而是对 π₀.₅、GR00T N1.7、VLA-Adapter 在 RTX 4090/H100 上做逐阶段 profile：把 ViT、VLM、AE 分开测量 GEMM/TCU/L2/功耗，比较 batching 与 CUDA streams / green contexts 的 stage co-execution。作者发现 AE 内存受限、weight-loading 是瓶颈，batching 能改善 AE 利用率；但 ViT/VLM 本身是 compute-bound GEMM，批处理会显著增加延迟；co-execution 吞吐提升仅 1.02–1.23×，因为 VLM GEMM 阻塞 AE kernel 调度，或在分区 SM 上变慢。与已有 LLM serving 直接迁移不同，本文给出逐阶段账本。证据分级：arXiv HTML 片段，作者实验自述，数值未独立复现。启示：多客户端调度不能只按请求批处理，需按 AE/VLM 异质性决定是否批、何时抢占；action chunking 天然支持时间交织，但一旦超出 GPU idle 预算，仍需异步/可中断的系统控制面。未查证其调度器实现。

**2. 潜在世界模型 + 残差策略做 VLA-MBRL**
《Efficient VLA Reinforcement Learning via Subchunk Rollouts in Latent World Models》，2026-11-23，arXiv cs.LG，https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27645

旧问题：图像/视频世界模型的 VLA-MBRL 计算开销大；潜在世界模型有递推误差，且预测 latent 与 VLA 所需的视觉输入接口不匹配。核心机制：LS-MBPO 用 Hierarchical Forcing 训练潜在世界模型——窗口内稠密因果监督加跨窗口自回归反馈；Latent Subchunk Rollouts 冻结预训练 VLA，把其输出 action chunk 切成 subchunk 作基础动作，训练轻量潜在残差策略逐步修正；Progress-Conditioned Branch-Start Curriculum 将 rollout 起点从任务后期逐步移到早期。作者报告 LIBERO Long 成功率 71.2%，对比 VLA-MBPO 64.4%；世界模型训练用 4×RTX 5090，RL 单 RTX 5090，而对比方法用 4×H100。注意硬件不同，不能直接折算加速比。与已有路线差别：不生成像素未来，不全参微调 VLA，仅训练残差策略和价值网络。证据分级：arXiv HTML 片段，作者实验自述，基准配置未独立核验。启示：把长 action chunk 当作策略先验，再局部重规划，可能降低 VLA 查询频率；训练系统只需更新小 head，降低显存与周期。关键待验证：残差策略与冻结 VLA 的 subchunk 一致性在不同 embodiment 上是否稳定。

**3. 机器人 Agent 给策略写“中断程序”**
《Tripwire: Robot Agents that Program Their Own Interrupts under Human Disturbance》，2026-11-23，arXiv cs.CV，https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27182

旧问题：turn-based harness 在策略调用返回前锁死 agent；人类突然进入路径或目标任务被移动时，VLA 无法及时重新决策。频繁唤醒 agent 很贵，但多数控制步骤不需要新高层决策。核心机制：TRIP 是训练无关 harness；agent 每次调用附带一个 stateful Python tripwire，可查询小型 VLM 定位人、测距，并结合深度、记忆、计时器判断是否触发；触发时先 stop-and-hold 再唤醒 agent，自述停止开销约 0.24s，不等 agent 推理。Agent 收到 firing reason 后重写 tripwire（例如从“人靠近”改成“人离开”）。作者在 RoboHD 168 个扰动场景报告：最强策略安全率从 61.3% 提升到 81.3%，任务成功率 38.7% vs 31.0%；实机两任务 25/40，turn-based 5/40，policy alone 1/40。与已有路线差别：不是 VoLo 式固定周期轮询，也不是 DoReMi 式二值约束检查，而是可计算、可更新的中断程序。证据分级：arXiv HTML 片段，作者自述；实机样本有限，扰动分布需核验。启示：安全闭环应把事件检测（小 VLM）与策略推理（大 VLA）解耦；GPU 服务需给监控查询高优先级或并行流，触发时能抢占当前 VLA 执行。这是类似 CPU 中断/看门狗的控制面设计。

**4. 3D VLA 的 2D/3D 联合 token 剪枝**
《2D or 3D? Rethinking Token Pruning in 3D VLAs with Cross-Modal Correlation Awareness》，v3 于 2026-11-23 更新，arXiv cs.RO，https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.09244（首版日期未查证）

旧问题：3D VLA 同时处理图像与点云 token，推理成本高；现有剪枝看单 token 重要性，未显式考虑 2D/3D 冗余、互补与跨 patch 耦合。核心机制：先分析 inner-patch 的 Interaction Correlation、Conditional Correlation，以及邻域 Inter-Patch Entropy 和剪枝引起的耦合；然后 Correlation-Aware Candidate State Modeling 评估每个 patch 在保留双模态/仅 2D/仅 3D/全不保留下的动作相关信息，单模态保留时用跨模态预测残差补偿；Correlation-Guided Pruning Search 按邻域熵探索局部 outlier；Coupling-Aware Pruning Optimization 在每次交换后更新受影响成本；最后用 fused GPU kernel 把选中 token pack 成短序列。作者报告 MLA 加速 2.06–2.10×、FiS-VLA 1.86–1.91×，成功率仅降 0.5–0.6 pp。与已有路线差别：不依赖单个注意力分数，而是直接建模联合保留状态与邻域熵。证据分级：arXiv HTML 片段，作者实验自述；成功率下降是否统计显著未说明。启示：3D VLA 的视觉 token 压缩需要跨模态耦合感知，fused pack kernel 可把剪枝后的序列重排下沉到 CUDA；对 GPU 推理，这是 prefill 前的新增前置 kernel，需要与主干 GEMM 联合调度。

**5. 从多步去噪蒸馏到一步世界动作模型**
《DIDO: Distilling Interaction-Centric Dynamics into One-Step Denoising for World Action Models》，v4 于 2026-11-23 更新，arXiv cs.RO，https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15570（首版日期未查证）

旧问题：WAM 依赖迭代视频去噪，闭环控制延迟高；简单截断成一步会保留静态背景，但丢失后期才出现的 gripper–object 交互动态。核心机制：DIDO 显示去噪存在时空不对称——静态结构早形成，交互区动态逐步显现。方法上，用 Distribution Matching Distillation 把四步教师压成单步 generator；加入 interaction-centric visual reasoning token，显式建模 gripper、目标物体与交互，并用未来 bounding-box 轨迹监督；目标物体多层表示与预训练 DINOv3 特征对齐；第二阶段 mixture-of-transformers 动作专家直接读取世界模型中间表示，不 decode/re-encode 视频。作者报告相对 Fast-WAM-IDM 端到端延迟由 871ms 降到 108ms，LIBERO 99.0%、LIBERO-Plus 76.3%、RoboTwin 91.9%；摘要与正文存在 0.1–0.3pp 差异，未核验。与已有路线差别：不是去掉未来想象，也不是普通 one-step truncation，而是显式恢复晚现交互动态。证据分级：arXiv HTML 片段，作者实验自述；DMD 训练代价与模型尺寸未详。启示：迭代去噪 WAM 可能被单步蒸馏逼近，但 GPU kernel 从多步调度变成单次大前向；需重新 profile 单步模型的 GEMM 占用与显存。仍需检验分布外长时序任务下交互动态是否保持。

**6. 前向触觉 VLA：把代理损失与物理量配对**
《FORTH: Grounding Tactile VLA Execution via Forward-Only Proxy-Control Pairing》，2026-11-23，arXiv cs.RO，https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26744；代码自述开源于 https://github.com/Jordanlllll/FORTH

旧问题：触觉 VLA 常用代理损失最小化外推力控能力，但代理目标与物理可观测未成对；冻结视觉 backbone 丢弃接触几何；反向传播在边缘设备内存高。核心机制：三层 paired evaluation protocol。Representation 层用两个 Forward-Forward 块的层局部触觉 trunk，不反向传播；Update 层用 rank-8 token-parallel zeroth-order adapter，在 4-bit 冻结 backbone 的 action head 上做激活空间更新，自述每次更新 16 个前向（T=8 tokens）；Controller 层 SlipGuard 连续 shear-ratio gate + 两帧 debounced 校正，在即将滑移时触发。作者报告 elasto-plastic shell 上峰值抓取力为 reflex ramp 的 1/29，LIBERO 三套平均成功率 97.6%，峰值激活内存比反向传播步骤低 7.12×。与已有路线差别：不是单独 forward-only 或 zeroth-order，而是强制每个算法代理量与物理量成对报告、符号一致。证据分级：arXiv HTML 片段，作者实验自述；代码链接存在但未验证；物理对象与基准代表性有限。启示：边缘 VLA 在线微调可考虑 zeroth-order/forward-only，降低更新内存；低层 SlipGuard 与高层 Tripwire 的多时间尺度事件门控，提示安全控制应分层叠加。真实硬件泛化仍待验证。

---

**跨领域弱信号**

今天材料共同弱信号是：VLA 不再被当作端到端黑箱，而是拆成“分层运行时”——慢速语义重规划（Tripwire、LS-MBPO subchunk）、中速策略生成（此前已见的 NAT VLA streaming chunk）、快速底层信号/世界动态门控（FORTH SlipGuard、DIDO interaction dynamics）。另一弱信号：VLA 的 GPU 利用率已独立成为研究问题，多客户端测量给出 AE/VLM 异质瓶颈，2Dor3D、DIDO 则从 token 剪枝和单步蒸馏入手降低单请求延迟。系统研究者开始把 VLA 视作“短前向 + 固定长度 AE”的负载，而不是 LLM 的 decode。

**趋势假设（非验证结论）**

1. VLA serving 将出现按阶段异质性调度的控制面，支持抢占和事件触发，而不只是 continuous batching。置信度中高。可反证：在 warehouse 多机器人场景中，若抢占/监控导致任务成功率下降，或 GPU 吞吐不优于静态 batching，则假设不成立。
2. 冻结 VLA + 轻量残差/潜在世界模型将成为中低成本策略改进的主流，而非全参数 post-training。置信度中。可反证：在统一 benchmark 上，若残差/潜在世界模型相对全参数 RL 成功率差距大且样本效率优势不明显，假设弱化。
3. 安全要求会推动训练无关的“可编程中断”成为 VLA 部署外层。置信度中高。可反证：在遮挡/陌生扰动下，若小 VLM 监控漏检或误触发明显增加，说明该外层的感知鲁棒性有限。

**本周值得精读的 2 篇**

- Multi-Client Inference Techniques for Vision-Language-Action Models：https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26944（VLA 服务调度的系统测量基础）
- Tripwire: Robot Agents that Program Their Own Interrupts under Human Disturbance：https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27182（事件驱动控制面与异步安全，适合 VLA 运行时系统设计）

---
**本次采集**：共采集 1540 条，去重后 1176 条；候选池 120 条，本次精选 6 条。源异常 1 处（见仓库 Actions 日志）。

selected.text: Analysis of Multi-Client Inference Techniques for Vision-Language-Action Models Anonymous Author(s) Stefan de Lasa Affiliation: University of Toronto Mohammadreza Mofayezi Affiliation: University of Toronto Gennady Pekhimenko Affiliation: University of Toronto Nandita Vijaykumar Affiliation: University of Toronto Abstract Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) are a new class of machine learning model for generalizable robot control. While they enable robots to perform complex tasks in unseen environments, serving VLAs leaves hardware idle between inference passes and under-utilized during inference. Serving multiple clients at once can improve utilization, but fundamental multi-client techniques such as batching and co-execution have not been characterized for VLAs. We therefore characterize the trade-offs these known techniques impose across latency, throughput, power, and hardware utilization. Our findings inform trade-offs and challenges for future multi-VLA serving systems. I Introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] are an emerging paradigm in robotics that aim to learn generalizable robotics behavior. They leverage internet-scale vision encoders (ViT) and vision-language models (VLM) as backbones to understand image observations and user text-prompt instructions. A subsequent “action expert” (AE) stage generates a series of actions to achieve the text-prompted goal (see Figure 1 ). Fig. 1 : Overview of VLA models. Fig. 2 : Illustration of VLA inference and action execution. Unlike stand-alone VLMs, VLAs typically follow the ViT encoding and VLM prefill stages with a constant-step diffusion-based action policy [ 1 , 2 ] , rather than a variable-length auto-regressive decode [ 4 , 5 ] . The VLA “action chunking” paradigm entails that multiple action tokens are generated per inference pass, instead of a single decoded language token like with large-language models (LLMs) or VLMs. As a result, VLA workloads alternate between GPU inference and on-robot action execution (see Figure 2 ). While VLAs have improved robotic generalizability [ 1 , 6 ] , we find they severely under-utilize GPU compute. Action chunking leaves the GPU idle between inference passes for > > 80% of total task completion time while the robot executes generated actions. We also observe under-utilization during inference passes: streaming multiprocessor (SM) throughput averages 21-27% across models, with the AE’s utilization being the lowest of all three stages (5-19%). Given the high cost of GPUs, VLA operators are economically motivated to maximize hardware utilization [ 7 ] . Since single-robot scenarios leave hardware idle, multi-client VLA serving – scheduling inference for multiple robotic clients on one device – is a natural setting to study. This setting is most applicable to warehouse and factory deployments where robot fleets communicate with an on-premises server [ 8 ] . Multi-client serving enables techniques such as batching [ 5 , 4 ] and stage co-execution [ 9 , 10 ] to improve inference-time utilization, but these have not been characterized for VLAs. Prior LLM/VLM serving work [ 5 , 4 , 10 , 9 ] does not account for the VLA’s AE or action chunking, and prior multi-client VLA work [ 8 , 11 ] details neither the heterogeneous behavior of VLA stages nor stage co-execution. We profile popular VLA models [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , spanning key VLA architectural axes, to highlight fundamental challenges with these serving techniques applied to VLAs. Our analysis of batching shows that it alone cannot improve utilization across all stages due to the VLM’s and ViT’s compute-bound matrix-multiplication (GEMM) kernels. Furthermore, intuitions from LLM serving do not transfer directly to VLAs, since the latter cannot easily amortize the increased latency incurred from a batched VLM and ViT. Stage co-execution yields modest speedups as VLM GEMM kernels block AE kernel dispatching or slow substantially on partitioned SMs. Therefore, in this characterization study, we make the following contributions: • We explain VLA GPU compute under-utilization, both between and during inference passes, motivating the multi-client setting we characterize. • We analyze VLA per-stage hardware utilization, power usage, and latency under batching, quantifying trade-offs and fundamental challenges for multi-client VLA serving. • We explain the behavior of VLAs under stage co-execution, highlighting the limitations of co-execution techniques. II Methodology II-A VLA Models We profile three popular open-source VLA models: π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 1 ] , GR00T N1.7 [ 2 ] , and VLA-Adapter [ 3 ] using the compilation methods from their respective implementations. The models span key VLA architectural axes: parameter scale (0.5-3B), action-generation mechanism (flow-matching, L1-regression), and VLM-AE interface (full KV cache, single embedding, per-layer cross-attention), as summarized in Table I . TABLE I: Profiled VLA models. All are fine-tuned for the DROID [ 12 ] platform and run with two camera views. π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} GR00T N1.7 VLA-Adapter VLM PaliGemma Cosmos-Reason2 Prismatic (Gemma) (Qwen3-VL) (Qwen2.5) VLM/ViT params 3B 2B 0.5B AE flow-match. flow-match. L1-reg. AE params 300M 1B 100M VLM-AE interf. full KV single per-layer cache embedding cross-attn. II-B Evaluation Methodology To reduce variability, our experiments report averages over 100 runs (fewer for NCU utilization measurements) after five warm-up runs. We input random images and use a short text prompt (40 tokens). Our measurements use CUDA synchronization. Utilization metrics come from NVIDIA Nsight Compute [ 13 ] . II-C Hardware We profile each model on an NVIDIA RTX4090 and H100. The latter is a representative data-center GPU standard for LLM serving [ 4 ] . Although some VLAs have been adapted for deployment on embedded/onboard devices [ 14 ] , we target larger GPUs for two reasons. First, server-side network and inference latencies are lower than onboard inference latency in most scenarios [ 15 ] . Second, server-side GPUs enable larger models with further improved robot generalization [ 16 , 6 ] . III Inter-Request Idleness Generating and executing action chunks creates alternating idle-busy periods for the GPU (see Figure 2 ), which allows for multi-client scheduling [ 11 ] . In Figure 3 , we measure the effect that this action chunking has on GPU idleness. Fig. 3 : Percentage of time the GPU is idle, over different chunk sizes and control frequencies. Control frequency (in Hz) is the rate at which the robot executes actions. Figure 3 shows that the GPU is typically idle > > 80% of the time. This idleness arises because generating an additional action token adds minimal inference latency: increasing the chunk size from 10 to 75 raises latency by < < 10%. However, this same increase in chunk size corresponds to a 750% increase in action execution time on the robot. Therefore, action chunking leaves the GPU idle during the majority of each request cycle, even at high control frequencies and on consumer-grade GPUs. Because a single client occupies the GPU ∼ \sim 15% of the time, temporal interleaving alone can support ∼ \sim 5-10 clients before the GPU’s idle budget is consumed. Beyond that, additional clients’ compute periods must overlap, so utilization gains require techniques that share the GPU under contention, such as batching and co-execution. IV Multi-request Batching IV-A Utilization and Power Analysis GPUs are costly and consume substantial power. Consequently, VLA model operators have a strong economic incentive to maximize their utilization [ 7 ] . However, experiments reveal that VLA inference fails to saturate GPU compute, thereby raising the opportunity cost to serve these models. Batching, a fundamental technique in machine learning serving [ 17 , 5 ] , combines input tensors so as to better exploit the GPU’s parallel compute units and achieve higher utilization [ 5 ] . Figure 4 and Figure 5 measure the per-stage hardware utilization and power (respectively) of three VLA models as batch size increases. We make the following observations. Fig. 4 : Utilization metrics over different batch sizes for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , GR00T and VLA-Adapter. Profiled on RTX4090 and H100. Fig. 5 : Mean power per batch size of π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , GR00T and VLA-Adapter on an RTX4090. To isolate the switching activity factor, we hold the GPU’s clock frequency constant. First, at a batch size of 1, the AE’s compute utilization is low, with “SM Throughput %” ranging from 4.6 to 18.7%. Profiling π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} on an RTX4090 (representative case) shows that the AE’s most time-consuming kernels are GEMM kernels, yet the average “Tensor Active %” remains below 2%. Two factors account for this. First, a weight-loading bottleneck: these kernels have high memory throughput (70-80%) but low SM throughput (10%). Second, the stage’s key kernels are too small to saturate the GPU, as the AE computes attention over a short context, denoising a chunk of only 15 to 50 action tokens at once [ 1 ] while cross-attending to the VLM output. NCU profiling confirms this: the longest kernels run with low grid and block sizes. Because they issue too few instructions to overlap with outstanding memory requests, the weight-loading latency is exposed on the critical path. Second, TCU utilization increases with batch size. All model stages exhibit some gain, but the effect is largest for the AE. The greatest TCU throughput gains originate from feed-forward network (FFN) kernels. These kernels grow linearly with batch size [ 18 ] , allowing more warps to be scheduled and producing near-linear increases in TCU throughput. Third, Figure 5 shows that the power usage of the AE is characterized by the power required during the weight-loading bottleneck, which stays constant as batch size increases. For GR00T’s AE, which has higher TCU utilization at a batch size of 1, batching the AE incurs a power overhead ( ∼ \sim 1.5 × \times at a batch size of 4). Fourth, the VLM and ViT stages exhibit higher compute utilization than the AE. Attending to vision and text tokens yields a context length of 700 to 1000 tokens, which results in larger GEMM kernels with higher arithmetic intensity. VLM GEMMs are also larger than the AE’s since their parameter count is typically one order of magnitude larger. Our profile traces show that the VLM’s execution time is dominated by FFN GEMM kernels (65% of time). Batching therefore has little effect on VLM compute utilization, as these time-dominating kernels already have high compute utilization at a batch size of one. Fifth, L2 throughput increases with batch size for nearly all models and stages, since the larger GEMM kernels produced by batching exhibit greater data reuse through tiling [ 19 ] . Together, these results demonstrate that batching improves utilization primarily for the AE, while the backbone’s utilization remains largely unchanged. Therefore, increasing overall utilization cannot be achieved through batching alone. IV-B Latency Analysis Batching can increase latency when the unbatched workload already saturates the GPU’s compute units [ 17 ] . Because VLA response time is critical for safety and task completion [ 15 ] , serving providers must balance utilization and throughput against latency. Yet, this trade-off has not been quantified for each VLA stage. In Figure 6 we measure the per-stage latency overhead of batching and make the following observations. Fig. 6 : Per-batch latency for all models on RTX and H100 GPUs. Standard deviation bars are shown but are usually < ⁣ ± <\pm 1ms. First, the AE batches with minimal latency overhead (1.15-1.33 × \times at batch size 4, H100). The action-stage kernels perform relatively little computation and are memory-bound. Thus, once model weights are loaded, generating an additional batch of tokens adds little latency. The AE’s low TCU utilization (Figure 4 ) means that large batches cause minimal extra stalling on the math pipeline. Second, the VLM and ViT stages benefit less from batching, with much smaller throughput gains than the AE. In π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ’s VLM, > > 65% of time is spent on dense FNN GEMM kernels (batch size 1), and > > 50% of cycles stall on the math pipeline. Larger batches only deepen this compute bottleneck, raising latency. Batching therefore affects VLA stages unevenly. The ViT and VLM process larger token counts, producing GEMM kernels that grow with batch size and dominate end-to-end latency (44-71% at batch size 4). A Preprint 1 Introduction World models [ 24 , 26 ] provide a promising avenue for improving vision-language-action (VLA) policies through model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) [ 10 ] , as they enable the generation of imagined experiences for policy optimization while reducing reliance on costly real-world interactions. Recent approaches [ 26 , 28 , 18 ] have primarily explored this direction by leveraging large-scale generative world models to predict future observations in the pixel space. However, generating high-dimensional visual observations introduces substantial computational overhead, while pixel-level prediction does not necessarily provide the compact state representations most suitable for downstream policy learning. Latent world models offer a promising alternative by modeling environment dynamics directly in a compact representation space, avoiding the need for explicit future image generation. Moreover, recent advances in latent world modeling, such as LeWorldModel [ 14 ] , demonstrate the potential of learning task-relevant representations that capture essential information for downstream decision-making. These properties make latent world models particularly appealing for developing more computationally efficient MBRL frameworks for VLA policies. Figure 1: Overview of LS-MBPO. (1) LS-MBPO first trains a latent world model to predict future latents with Hierarchical Forcing. (2) LS-MBPO uses Latent Subchunk Rollout to generate imagined experiences with a residual policy attached to a frozen VLA. (3) A success detector is trained to reward the imagined rollouts, with which a residual policy is optimized using TD3 + BC. Despite these advantages, integrating latent world models into VLA-based MBRL remains challenging due to two fundamental challenges. First, latent world models suffer from compounding prediction errors [ 20 , 10 , 22 ] during recursive rollouts. Existing approaches [ 27 , 14 ] typically train latent dynamics using one-step prediction objectives, where predictions are conditioned on ground-truth latent histories. However, during imagined rollouts, the model must recursively take its own predictions as inputs, creating a discrepancy between training and inference conditions. Prediction errors at earlier steps can propagate to subsequent predictions, while the resulting deviations in latent inputs may further amplify these errors, leading to increasingly unreliable imagined trajectories. Second, there exists a mismatch between the interfaces of latent world models and pretrained VLAs. Latent world models predict future states in compact latent spaces, whereas pretrained VLAs typically require visual observations as inputs, making it difficult to directly use predicted latent states for subsequent action generation. Besides the interface mismatch, existing VLA-MBRL approaches, such as VLA-MBPO [ 26 ] , often rely on fine-tuning all VLA parameters using imagined experiences. Such full-parameter optimization introduces substantial computational and memory overhead, which undermines the computational advantage of using latent world models for policy learning. These challenges raise an important question: how can we leverage latent imagination for VLA reinforcement learning while ensuring reliable recursive prediction and computationally efficient policy optimization? To address these challenges, we propose L atent S ubchunk Rollout for MBPO (LS-MBPO), a lightweight residual model-based reinforcement learning framework for VLA using latent world models, which is shown in Fig. 1 . First, we introduce Hierarchical Forcing to improve the reliability of latent dynamics under recursive prediction. It combines dense causal prediction supervision within each temporal window with autoregressive feedback across consecutive windows, enabling the world model to progressively adapt to its own predictions while mitigating compounding errors. Second, we propose Latent Subchunk Rollouts to bridge the interface gap between pretrained VLAs and latent world models. Specifically, we freeze the pretrained VLA and divide its generated action chunk into shorter subchunks as base actions, while training a lightweight residual policy conditioned on the current latent state and the corresponding base actions. During imagination, the residual policy progressively refines the base actions based on the updated latent states predicted by the world model. In this way, a single VLA query provides a behavioral prior for multiple successive residual decisions, allowing the policy to be optimized through the lightweight residual policy and value network. Furthermore, we introduce a Progress-Conditioned Branch-Start Curriculum that gradually shifts the sampling distribution from states near task completion to earlier task stages, enabling more efficient learning from imagined rollouts. On LIBERO Long, LS-MBPO completes the world model training on 4 RTX 5090s and the RL stage on a single RTX 5090 with a success rate of 71.2%, compared with 64.4% for VLA-MBPO trained on 4 H100 GPUs, demonstrating a practical route towards resource-efficient VLA policy improvement. Our contributions are as follows: First, we propose LS-MBPO, a lightweight residual model-based reinforcement learning framework for improving VLA with latent world models. To our knowledge, this is the first work attempting to integrate VLA with latent world models for model-based RL. Second, we address two core limitations of VLA-MBRL in latent world models, i.e., compounding error and interface mismatch by proposing Hierarchical Forcing and Latent Subchunk Rollouts. Finally, through extensive experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin and a real-world ALOHA robot, we demonstrate that LS-MBPO not only improves sample efficiency but also achieves superior policy performance, offering a practical solution to efficient VLA reinforcement learning through latent imagination. 2 Related Works 2.1 World Models for Visual Control World models have been widely explored for visual control by learning action-conditioned environment dynamics. Early approaches, such as Visual Foresight [ 3 ] , predict future visual observations to support planning. Advances in generative modeling have enabled increasingly general and realistic world simulation: UniSim [ 23 ] learns an interactive simulator supporting vision-language planning and reinforcement learning, while NVIDIA Cosmos [ 15 ] demonstrates the potential of large-scale video models for physical world simulation and synthetic data generation. However, synthesizing high-dimensional visual observations incurs substantial computational overhead, and visual fidelity alone does not guarantee representations suited to downstream control. In parallel, latent world models learn action-conditioned dynamics in compact representation spaces, supporting planning and policy learning without decoding images during imagined rollouts. Representative methods, including PlaNet [ 7 ] , Dreamer [ 6 ] , and TD-MPC [ 9 ] , demonstrate the effectiveness of latent-space imagination for model-based control. More recent methods [ 16 , 27 , 14 , 12 , 25 ] further explore visual control through predictive dynamics over pretrained visual features and jointly learned representations. These advances motivate investigating how latent-space imagination can support efficient reinforcement learning of VLA policies while remaining compatible with their visual observation interfaces. 2.2 Reinforcement Learning for VLA Models Recent works have explored reinforcement learning to improve pretrained VLA policies. Model-based reinforcement learning further enables VLA policies to learn from imagined experiences generated by world models. WMPO [ 28 ] leverages generative world models to perform policy optimization through imagined rollouts. selected.title: Tripwire: Robot Agents that Program Their Own Interrupts under Human Disturbance
selected.summary: arXiv:2611.27182v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agent harnesses are turn-based: the agent acts, waits for the result, then reasons. When the action invokes a pretrained robot policy, such as a vision-language-action (VLA) or world action model (WAM), the policy may react continuously to observations, but the agent cannot revisit its decision until the call returns. Meanwhile, a person may step into the robot's path or move the object it is about to grasp. Invoking the agent more often narrows this blind interval, but a reasoning model takes seconds per decision and most control steps need no new one. We propose TRIP, a training-free, event-driven harness in which the agent programs its own interrupts. With each call, the agent writes a tripwire: a lightweight, stateful Python program that runs alongside the policy, can query a compact VLM (for example, to locate a person and measure their distance), and decides whether the call continues or control returns to the agent. When it fires, the harness halts the policy and returns control with the reason; the agent then reassesses, adapts, and continues under a rewritten tripwire. We evaluate TRIP with three VLAs and one WAM on RoboHD, a benchmark of 168 RoboCasa365 scenes in which a simulated person disturbs the robot and any human-robot contact counts as failure. Compared with a turn-based harness using the same agent and tools, TRIP halves the rate of human contact with the strongest policy, raising safety from 61.3% to 81.3%, without sacrificing task success (38.7% vs. 31.0%). Real-robot experiments show that TRIP completes two manipulation tasks under human interference where the turn-based harness and the policy alone largely fail.

Invoking the agent more often narrows this blind interval, but a reasoning model takes seconds per decision and most control steps need no new one. Figure 1 : TRIP in one episode with Xiaomi-Robotics-1, while a person mops past the robot. A tripwire fires when the person comes within 0.3 m of the base, and the agent backs the robot out of the way, then resumes the policy under a tripwire on the person’s new position. When that one fires at the spot the person has just left, the agent rewrites it to watch for a close or reaching person, and the policy finishes the task. Top: when the agent, the policy and each (simplified) tripwire run. 1 Introduction Frontier vision-language models increasingly act as agents for robots: they interpret scenes, decompose tasks, and coordinate execution through tool calls [ 47 , 54 , 11 , 45 ] . A common harness exposes a pretrained manipulation policy as a callable skill and invokes the agent again only when the call returns [ 57 ] . This turn-based interface locks the agent out while the policy runs, even though an action chosen at the start of a call can become unsafe or obsolete before it finishes. If a person steps into the robot’s path mid-execution, the agent remains blind to the disturbance until control is handed back. The policy’s own closed loop does not remove this blind spot. Vision-language-action (VLA) models [ 3 , 22 , 2 ] and world action models (WAMs) [ 55 ] can react to new observations, but strong performance when nothing interferes with the task does not guarantee reliable behavior around people. In a shared kitchen, someone may move the target plate or close the fridge door the robot has just opened. When we augment RoboCasa365 tasks [ 34 ] with a reactive human avatar, all four pretrained policies we evaluate lose more than half of their successes; the strongest drops from 61.9% to 20.8% and touches the person in roughly half of all episodes. The agent can interpret such disturbances and choose a response, but it needs timely access to the changing scene. Querying it more frequently incurs substantial computation, and each high-level decision still requires an inference call that can take seconds [ 47 , 54 ] . Watching the scene does not require strong reasoning: noticing that a person has come close is a perception problem that a compact VLM and a depth image settle in a fraction of a second. Existing systems watch a running call in one of three ways. VoLo [ 10 ] polls a frontier model every few seconds. DoReMi [ 18 ] asks a small VLM whether language constraints written by the planner still hold: it can look for anything the planner names, but it gets back only yes or no. Code-as-Monitor [ 60 ] runs generated code over geometric states tracked from the start of a subgoal, without issuing new VLM queries during execution. Reacting to a person takes both: spotting someone who was not in the scene when the check was written, and judging from their distance and motion whether they matter. What should interrupt the agent also shifts with its latest decision. After judging that a nearby person does not obstruct the task, the agent resumes the policy and needs to hear only if the person comes closer; if it chooses to wait, it instead needs to know when the person leaves. We let the agent program the interrupt and update it as its decisions change. We introduce TRIP ( Fig. 1 ), a harness in which robot agents program their own interrupts. The agent attaches a tripwire to a tool call: a stateful Python program that runs alongside policy execution, direct robot motions, or waiting. A tripwire both looks and computes: it chooses which cameras to read and what to ask a compact VLM, such as where a person is, and combines the answer with depth, memory of earlier checks, and timers to decide whether to interrupt. When it fires, the harness halts the active call before waking the agent with the reason, so stopping costs one check (0.24 s on average on our real robot) and not an agent turn (4.3 s). The agent then resumes the policy, repositions the robot, or waits, updating the tripwire as needed so it wakes the agent again when the situation changes. Because the policy remains a black box, TRIP wraps pretrained VLAs and WAMs without fine-tuning. We evaluate TRIP in simulation with three VLAs and one WAM on RoboHD , a benchmark of 168 scenes built by adding a reactive human avatar to 42 RoboCasa365 tasks [ 34 ] . RoboHD covers spatial, object-state, task-state, and perceptual disturbances, and any human-robot contact counts as failure. With the strongest policy, Xiaomi-Robotics-1, TRIP raises safety, the fraction of episodes without human contact among the scenes that can be solved without the person, from 61.3% to 81.3% relative to a turn-based harness using the same agent, action tools, and prompt, halving human contact. Task success is 38.7% versus 31.0% with the person and 73.2% versus 73.8% without, while agent invocations decrease from 30.3 to 19.4 per minute of robot time. TRIP is also safer than the turn-based harness with each of the other three policies. An ablation with Xiaomi-Robotics-1 shows that keeping the initial tripwire unchanged lowers safety to 61.3%. On two real-robot tasks, hanging a mug and hanging a towel, TRIP succeeds in 25 of 40 trials across two disturbance conditions (blocking the arm and moving the target object), compared with 5 of 40 for the turn-based harness and 1 of 40 for the policy alone. Our contributions are: • TRIP , a training-free, policy-agnostic harness in which robot agents program their own interrupts: stateful tripwires that query a compact VLM during execution, compute on its answers, and are updated as the situation changes. • RoboHD , a human-disturbance benchmark of 168 scenes built on 42 RoboCasa365 tasks, where any human-robot contact counts as failure. • Experiments with three VLAs, one WAM, and a real robot: a matched comparison in which TRIP halves human contact with the strongest policy, an ablation on updating tripwires, and real-robot trials under disturbance. 2 Related Work Robot foundation models and agentic manipulation. Recent advances in robot foundation models have enabled increasingly general manipulation capabilities. Vision-language-action (VLA) models learn transferable policies from large-scale robot data [ 8 , 7 , 36 , 25 , 48 , 6 , 3 , 22 , 2 , 49 ] , with diffusion-based architectures [ 12 , 29 , 59 ] and multimodal conditioning [ 24 ] further expanding their capabilities. World action models extend this direction by jointly modeling actions and future observations [ 55 , 51 ] . Building on these pretrained models, language-model agents enable higher-level embodied reasoning [ 13 , 1 ] , program generation [ 28 , 44 , 20 ] , feedback-driven planning [ 21 , 42 , 56 , 30 ] , and policy orchestration [ 57 , 11 , 45 , 47 ] . However, in turn-based agentic harnesses, the agent typically regains control only after a tool call returns, limiting its ability to respond to changes during execution. TRIP addresses this limitation by allowing the agent to interrupt ongoing policy execution without modifying the underlying policy. Figure 2 : Overview of TRIP. Given an instruction ℓ \ell , the agent selects a call c c and a tripwire w w . The agent then reassesses the scene and updates the call and tripwire. Snowflakes denote frozen models; calls and VLM queries are illustrative. Runtime monitoring and event-driven control. Execution monitoring has been studied through language constraints, visual feedback, and generated programs [ 18 , 60 , 52 ] . DoReMi [ 18 ] detects plan-execution misalignment through visual checks, while Code-as-Monitor [ 60 ] evaluates generated spatiotemporal constraints. VoLo [ 10 ] periodically monitors running policies with a VLM, and The Harness [ 53 ] uses agent-written reactive guards. Event-triggered control similarly updates decisions when specified conditions hold [ 46 , 19 ] . TRIP enables agents to write and revise stateful interruption programs that combine on-demand VLM perception with depth, geometry, and temporal memory, determining when to return control to the agent. Human-robot interaction benchmarks. Manipulation benchmarks evaluate generalization across tasks, objects, and environments [ 23 , 33 , 17 , 31 , 40 , 15 , 62 ] , while recent work studies disturbances during execution [ 58 , 14 ] . selected.summary: arXiv:2604.09244v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: 3D vision-language-action (VLA) models process both image and point cloud tokens at each control step, increasing the cost of action prediction. Token pruning can reduce this cost, but a token's contribution depends on which other tokens remain. We present 2Dor3D, a framework that jointly selects which 2D and 3D tokens to retain under a fixed token budget. Our analysis shows that either modality can compensate for the other within a patch, that neighboring correlations help explain differences in pruning risk, and that shared tokens couple pruning decisions across patches. I Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions and have become an important paradigm for embodied intelligence [ 1 , 2 ] . Despite this progress, early VLA models relied primarily on 2D visual inputs [ 3 ] and still faced challenges in fine-grained manipulation [ 4 ] . Therefore, recent studies have explored 3D VLA models that jointly encode 2D images and 3D observations to improve spatial perception [ 5 , 6 ] . In 3D VLAs, 2D image tokens encode visual appearance and semantics, while 3D point cloud tokens capture geometric and spatial information [ 7 , 5 , 8 ] . Models such as MLA jointly process both modalities through shared attention [ 9 ] . Since both modalities describe the same physical scene, their representations exhibit both information overlap and modality-specific characteristics [ 10 ] , resulting in complex cross-modal correlations that reflect both redundancy and complementarity. However, joint reasoning over both modalities incurs substantial computational and memory overhead [ 11 ] . Token pruning reduces inference cost by shortening the visual token sequence processed by subsequent layers [ 12 ] . For 3D VLA models, identifying redundant tokens requires accounting for the information overlap and complementarity between 2D and 3D modalities. Related studies in 3D and multimodal vision assess token importance to guide pruning: Fast3D predicts global attention to estimate token importance [ 13 ] ; Geo3DPruner uses geometric correspondence to reduce cross-view redundancy [ 14 ] ; TokenFusion replaces uninformative tokens with features from other modalities for cross-modal fusion [ 15 ] . These studies demonstrate the effectiveness of using token importance to guide pruning and fusion. However, existing methods do not fully capture cross-modal information sharing and complementarity or inter-patch dependencies between 2D and 3D tokens, which we refer to as token correlations. Characterizing these correlations is key to distinguishing replaceable redundancy from irreplaceable features and guiding 2D/3D token pruning, but presents three challenges: Challenge ①: Within a patch, removing either the 2D or the 3D tokens alone may have little effect on the predicted action. These individual pruning costs do not reveal whether both modalities can be removed together or whether at least one must remain. Challenge ②: Even when two patches have similar cross-modal correlation scores, removing the same modality can affect their predicted actions differently. Assessing the pruning risk of a patch therefore requires understanding how its correlations are distributed across the surrounding neighborhood. Challenge ③: Shared tokens couple correlations across modalities and spatial patches. Pruning one token can therefore alter other correlations, making the joint impact of multiple pruning decisions difficult to assess and the global retention configuration difficult to determine. To address these challenges, we first analyze inner-patch and inter-patch 2D/3D correlations and then examine how these correlations are coupled across patches. Analysis ①: Across the four retention states of a patch, changes in action-related channels reveal how the two modalities interact and how much of the full response either can preserve on its own. We quantify these effects with Interaction Correlation and Conditional Correlation, respectively. Analysis ②: Two patches with nearly identical interaction scores can incur different pruning costs, motivating us to characterize their neighborhoods using Inter-Patch Entropy computed separately for interaction and conditional scores. Analysis ③: Pruning one token can alter correlations among the remaining tokens, so we extend the two metrics to these coupled relations to assess how one removal changes the cost of the next. Based on these insights, we propose 2Dor3D , a framework that jointly selects which image and point cloud tokens to retain under a fixed token budget. First, Correlation-Aware Candidate State Modeling estimates how much action-related information each patch retains with both modalities, 2D only, 3D only, or neither. When only one modality is retained, we predict the features of the other modality from it and transfer the prediction residual to the retained tokens. Second, Correlation-Guided Pruning Search uses neighborhood correlation scores and their entropy to explore more retention choices at local outliers. It discards candidates that cannot meet the token budget and ranks the rest by estimated information loss. Third, Coupling-Aware Pruning Optimization proposes exchanges between coupled regions and updates the affected pruning costs after each exchange to guide the next one. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We systematically analyze the conditionality, context dependence, and coupling of 2D/3D token correlations, revealing their implications for action prediction and joint pruning. • We propose 2Dor3D , which combines correlation modeling, guided search, and coupling-aware optimization to automatically determine 2D/3D token selection configurations under a budget. • We evaluate 2Dor3D on MLA and FiS-VLA using task success rate and end-to-end inference speedup in simulation, and task success rate and completion time on real robots. selected.summary: arXiv:2609.15570v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) use video generation models to predict future visual dynamics for robotic manipulation, but iterative denoising introduces additional latency for closed-loop control. One-step truncation reduces this cost, but risks discarding predictive information formed during later denoising steps. We empirically find that visual content converges at different rates during denoising: static scene structure forms early, whereas gripper–object interaction dynamics emerge progressively through subsequent steps. Consequently, one-step truncation preserves scene structure but loses late-emerging interaction dynamics useful for manipulation. Guided by this observation, we propose DIDO, which distills the converged dynamics of a multi-step video model into a single denoising step. By recovering interaction dynamics that would otherwise be lost through truncation, DIDO accelerates inference without sacrificing control performance. Moreover, DIDO introduces interaction-centric representation guidance to establish finer-grained, entity-level understanding of the recovered dynamic regions. Compared with Fast-WAM-IDM, DIDO reduces end-to-end inference latency by 87.6% (from 871 to 108 ms) while achieving higher success rates across multiple benchmarks. In general, DIDO achieves average success rates of 99.0% on LIBERO, 76.3% on LIBERO-Plus, and 91.9% on RoboTwin, while also demonstrating effective transfer to long-horizon and generalization tasks in real-world robotic manipulation. 1 Introduction Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) have achieved strong performance in robotic manipulation by leveraging large-scale vision-language pretraining to follow language instructions across diverse tasks and embodiments ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025b ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) . Most VLA policies predict actions directly from the current observation and language instruction, without explicitly modeling how the environment will evolve under the robot’s actions. Recently, World Action Models (WAMs) have explored a complementary direction by using video generation models to predict future visual dynamics ( Bai et al., 2026b ; Wu et al., 2024 ; Hu et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2026b ) . These predictions provide the policy with explicit foresight into how the robot, manipulated objects, and their interactions evolve over time. However, realizing such foresight at inference time remains computationally expensive because video generation typically relies on iterative denoising. A natural way to reduce this cost is to truncate the denoising process and extract predictive representations from only one or a few early steps ( Hu et al., 2025 ; Chi et al., 2025 ) . This substantially improves inference efficiency and has been shown to retain useful predictive information. Yet it remains unclear how much of the dynamics represented by the fully denoised video model are already present at these early steps. In particular, when denoising is reduced to a single step, what dynamics are preserved, and what dynamics are still missing? Figure 1: DIDO: interaction-centric dynamics in one step. The insight panel contrasts multi-step prediction, one-step truncation, and DIDO through decoded videos and latent dynamics, demonstrating that dynamics emerge progressively through subsequent steps and DIDO recover these dynamics in one step. The training panel summarizes interaction-centric distillation. The performance–efficiency panel compares success rates against inference latency on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin, highlighting DIDO’s strong performance at 108 ms. To answer this question, we conduct an empirical study of the denoising trajectory in Figure 1 , examining both decoded videos and latent representations. We observe a clear spatial and temporal asymmetry. After a single step, static background structure is already well formed, whereas the gripper and manipulated object remain blurry and poorly resolved. The same pattern appears in latent space: inter-frame changes in these interaction regions are weak at early steps but progressively strengthen and become spatially localized as denoising proceeds. These changes are concentrated around the gripper and manipulated object, whose evolving spatial relationship provides predictive cues for action selection. Naive single-step truncation therefore largely preserves scene structure but misses the interaction-centric dynamics that emerge later in denoising. Our denoising-stage analysis further shows that conditioning the action expert on later representations improves manipulation success. Together, these findings highlight the importance of interaction-centric dynamics for manipulation. We instantiate this insight in DIDO, a one-step World Action Model centered on recovering and better grounding interaction-centric dynamics. In Stage I, DIDO jointly combines distribution matching distillation (DMD) ( Yin et al., 2024 ) with interaction-centric visual reasoning. DMD transfers the converged dynamics of a multi-step video model into a single denoising step. Beyond recovering these dynamics, interaction-centric visual reasoning provides finer-grained, entity-level representations of the dynamic regions. Interaction-centric tokens, guided by future bounding-box trajectories, explicitly model the gripper, target object, and their evolving spatial relationship. Multi-layer alignment with target-object features from a pretrained DINOv3 encoder ( Siméoni et al., 2026 ) preserves discriminative visual information to support this entity-level modeling. Distillation and interaction-centric visual reasoning are jointly optimized in this stage. In Stage II, the resulting single-step world model is coupled with an action expert through a mixture-of-transformers architecture for closed-loop control. Overall, DIDO recovers interaction dynamics within a single denoising step, avoiding costly iterative denoising while maintaining or improving control performance. Ablations further show that interaction-centric guidance improves manipulation success, supporting the value of explicitly modeling these dynamic regions. The main contributions are threefold: 1. We reveal that static scene structure forms early during video denoising, while manipulation-relevant dynamics around the gripper and target object emerge progressively at later steps, and connect this observation to the control benefits of later denoising representations. 2. Guided by this finding, we develop DIDO to recover late-emerging dynamics in one step and explicitly structure them around manipulation-relevant entities, achieving efficient dynamics modeling for control. 3. Rather than merely preserving performance under one-step compression, DIDO achieves higher manipulation success rates while substantially reducing inference latency. Compared with Fast-WAM-IDM, which has the same model size and a similar architecture, DIDO reduces end-to-end latency by 87.6% (from 871 to 108 ms) while improving success rates across multiple benchmarks. DIDO achieves 99.0% on LIBERO, 76.3% on LIBERO-Plus, and 91.9% on RoboTwin, with effective transfer to real-world manipulation. 2 Related Work World Action Models for Robotic Manipulation. Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) have achieved strong performance in robotic manipulation ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025b ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Bai et al., 2026a ) . World Action Models (WAMs) explore a complementary direction by incorporating video-based future modeling into action prediction ( Ye et al., 2026b ; Li et al., 2026 ) . Early approaches synthesize future frames or subgoal images to guide action generation ( Du et al., 2023 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Tian et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2024 ) , while subsequent methods condition policies on predictive representations ( Hu et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Lyu et al., 2026 ) . Recent WAMs further couple video and action through joint generative modeling, latent action representations, or multi-stream architectures ( Cheang et al., 2024 ; Bi et al., 2026 ; Team et al., 2026b ) . Action-centered variants also use future visual dynamics primarily as training supervision or optional inference-time guidance ( Ye et al., 2026a ; Team et al., 2026a ) . Across these designs, a central question is which aspects of future dynamics are most useful for control. DIDO addresses this question by focusing on gripper–object interaction dynamics that emerge during later denoising steps and recovering them in a single step. Efficient World Action Models. Recent work improves WAM efficiency through several strategies. One line removes test-time future imagination entirely. Fast-WAM predicts actions without generating future observations ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) , eliminating the cost of explicit future prediction. A second line retains future modeling but truncates denoising, conditioning the policy on representations extracted from only one or a few early steps ( Chi et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) . Other approaches preserve future prediction while reducing architectural or conditioning overhead, for example by simplifying the action module, reusing future features across action denoising steps ( Ma et al., 2026 ) , or moving auxiliary geometric supervision to training time ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Closest to DIDO are methods that distill multi-step video or video-action predictions into one-step generation or predictive representations ( Akbari et al., 2026 ; Yan et al., 2026 ) . Within this line of work, DIDO uses interaction-centric supervision to guide what the one-step model preserves during distillation. Jointly optimized with distribution matching, trajectory and visual supervision encourage the distilled representations to retain manipulation-relevant entity dynamics and their coupled evolution. Object- and Interaction-Centric Representations for Manipulation. Object-centric VLA methods structure policy representations around task-relevant entities using visual prompts, object-conditioned features, slots and relations, or 3D object representations ( Li et al., 2025c ; Li et al., 2025a ; Hanyu et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026b ) . Recent WAMs extend this idea to future prediction by modeling object masks ( Yu et al., 2026 ; Lou et al., 2026 ) , temporally persistent robot/object slots ( Liu et al., 2026a ) , or structured semantic, geometric, and kinematic foresight ( Yan et al., 2026 ; Jin et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026b ; Ji et al., 2025 ) . While these approaches make future prediction increasingly object- and structure-aware, robot–object interactions are still largely represented implicitly. DIDO instead adopts interaction-centric visual reasoning, explicitly integrating gripper–object trajectories with visual representations during video generation to capture manipulation-relevant dynamics. 3 Method DIDO centers on interaction-centric dynamics: recovering them within a single denoising step, grounding them in manipulation-relevant entities, and efficiently exploiting them for action prediction. selected.title: FORTH: Grounding Tactile VLA Execution via Forward-Only Proxy-Control Pairing
selected.summary: arXiv:2611.26744v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are widely credited with force control, operating on the unverified assumption that proxy loss minimization implies physical force grounding. In this work, we demonstrate that this assumption breaks down at three core deployment levels: frozen visual backbones discard contact geometry, downstream losses mask token-level gradient alignment, and discrete indicators trigger optimization collapse. To address these disconnections, we present FORTH, a forward-only measurement harness and execution framework that explicitly pairs the optimization objective at each level with its physical control observable. FORTH incorporates three grounded pillars: a layer-local, forward-only tactile encoder that preserves spatial contact geometry without backpropagation, a token-parallel zeroth-order adapter enabling activation-space updates, and SlipGuard, a continuous tactile verification gate that fires on incipient slip. On an elasto-plastic structural shell, FORTH's closed-loop gate peaks at 29 times lower grip force than a monotone reflex ramp, preventing structural crush where the baseline leaves permanent deformation. Furthermore, FORTH matches state-of-the-art execution performance with a 97.6% average success rate across three evaluated LIBERO suites, while reducing peak activation memory by 7.12 times compared to a backpropagated step on the same backbone. Enhanced perception enables deeper physical intelligence.

To operate effectively under contact, state-of-the-art systems increasingly augment pretrained visual backbones with tactile or force sensing modalities [ 40 , 41 , 16 , 87 ] . Concurrently, tactile sensing hardware and representations have matured: optical tactile sensors, high-fidelity contact simulators, and learned representations provide policies with spatially resolved contact maps rather than scalar load readings [ 37 , 71 , 77 , 20 , 80 ] . While an emerging family of tactile VLAs reports force-aware execution across tasks like insertion, wiping, and grasping [ 11 , 2 , 8 , 49 , 90 , 10 , 84 , 86 , 52 , 51 , 35 , 88 ] , performance across these systems is predominantly evaluated using a single proxy metric per task level. Such scalar metrics obscure the underlying physical reality: the critical quantities governing whether an object survives an episode are rarely measured or reported together. This discrepancy stems from a missing evaluation and reporting convention. Existing research programs address isolated compute and memory bottlenecks without closing this measurement gap. Layer-local learning objectives replace global backpropagation with forward-only computations [ 23 , 38 , 44 , 65 , 29 , 55 , 63 , 36 , 17 , 61 , 1 ] , yet report performance strictly via local loss values. Zeroth-order (ZO) and gradient-free optimizers trade memory-intensive backward passes for forward queries [ 48 , 46 , 66 , 32 , 9 , 19 , 85 , 67 , 81 ] , evaluating only estimated gradient directional alignment. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) and quantization constrain these updates within frozen backbones [ 26 , 13 , 25 ] , while low-level controllers treat physical slip as a binary classification target scored by detection accuracy. Crucially, an improvement in these algorithmic proxies can decouple from physical interaction quality—a lower local loss does not inherently prevent object damage—and no current benchmark protocol [ 42 , 50 , 30 , 47 , 91 , 45 , 57 , 12 , 58 , 34 , 79 , 22 , 74 ] systematically measures and reports these paired dynamics. To resolve this decoupling, we introduce forth , a unified harness governed by a paired metric convention across all three execution levels: report the optimized algorithmic quantity alongside the physical quantity it aims to control, accepting a policy level only when both metrics move in lockstep. Operating entirely forward-only and layer-locally on frozen 4-bit backbones without global backward passes, forth integrates three key components: (1) a tactile feature trunk composed of two Forward-Forward (FF) blocks; (2) a token-parallel zeroth-order adapter of rank 8 attached to the action head; and (3) SlipGuard , a one-class shear-ratio gate with a bounded real-time corrector. Rather than introducing a massive new backbone, forth makes tactile policy execution measurable and correctable directly on edge deployment hardware, requiring only 16 forward passes per update ( T = 8 T{=}8 tokens) instead of full backpropagation. This design yields a deployment-ready harness that acts dynamically before manipulation failure occurs. Empirically, the forward-only tactile trunk matches backpropagated representation accuracy; the zeroth-order updater fine-tunes the rank-8 adapter at a fraction of backward memory requirements; and SlipGuard converts incipient slip into a recoverable interaction across three slip severity regimes, where standard hand-tuned force ramps result in permanent object crush. Figure 1 illustrates our testbed for recording physical contact dynamics across three material bodies driven past their friction limits. 2 Related Work 2.1 Vision-Language-Action Policies Vision-language-action models predict an action sequence from an image and an instruction [ 33 , 3 , 5 ] . Their scale comes from a pretrained multimodal backbone rather than from robot data, and the head that turns features into commands is small enough to adapt on one GPU. Alongside them sit action-chunking transformers for low-cost bimanual teleoperation [ 89 ] , tokenizers that compress a chunk to a short sequence [ 62 ] and open-world variants of the recipe [ 28 , 82 , 27 ] . Touch enters that stack in three ways: as semantic-aligned tokens projected into the same space as text [ 11 ] , as a residual representation added to a frozen visual policy [ 86 ] , or as a predictive model that forecasts contact before it occurs [ 90 , 84 , 31 ] . Neighboring designs fuse heterogeneous tactile sensors behind one policy [ 35 , 40 ] , learn the touch representation from future visual supervision [ 10 ] , or name material and object properties from touch without closing a control loop [ 83 ] . A separate line learns force implicitly rather than conditioning on it [ 41 , 21 ] : grip strength emerges from the task reward [ 59 , 60 , 8 ] , and the force in the logs is whatever the policy found sufficient. 2.2 Forward-Only Update Rules Forward-only learning replaces the backward pass with a local objective. Forward-Forward trains each layer on its own contrastive goodness [ 23 ] , and the similarity kernel of layer representations contracts toward rank one with depth [ 78 ] . Local error signals and forward gradients are the neighboring non-contrastive route [ 55 , 63 ] ; contrastive, predictive-coding and scalable variants extend it [ 1 , 61 , 17 , 36 ] . On hardware, INT8, sparse, binary-stochastic and closed-box trainers report lower energy, memory or compute than backpropagation at the edge [ 44 , 65 , 29 , 38 , 72 ] . Zeroth-order optimization estimates a descent direction from function evaluations alone, from the black-box attack estimator [ 7 ] and random search [ 48 , 66 ] through adaptive moments [ 9 ] to MeZO [ 46 ] , with variance-reduced variants [ 19 ] and convergence analyses [ 85 ] . Applications reach VLA adaptation [ 32 ] , quantized fine-tuning [ 67 ] and prompt tuning [ 81 ] . These methods are judged by downstream loss or recall. A population argument, in which independent per-token perturbations average out, predicts that estimator quality improves with token count; that prediction has not been measured against the true gradient on a physical signal. Adaptation and evaluation practice supply the rest: low-rank and quantized adapters [ 26 , 13 , 25 ] , one-bit backbones [ 76 ] , benchmarks and simulators [ 42 , 50 , 30 , 79 , 45 , 57 , 53 ] , and replication practice [ 56 , 75 , 43 ] . 2.3 Slip Detection and Tactile Sensing Slip detection has a reflex-control literature that predates learned policies. Visuo-tactile classifiers run on multi-scale temporal convolutions [ 18 ] , and incipient-slip measurement tracks the transition during in-hand pivoting [ 39 , 64 , 4 , 73 ] . Geometric reconstruction recovers extrinsic contact from touch and proprioception [ 52 ] , and the same contact signal drives sub-millimeter insertion [ 51 ] . A second class puts that signal in a fast loop under a slow planner: a reactive dexterous controller [ 54 , 2 ] , or a vibration signal routed straight to action [ 49 ] . On the representation side the split is between an online-refined tactile prediction that absorbs contact drift [ 87 ] and a decomposition that separates force from surface texture [ 88 ] . Both matter for the representation level: an aggregate can be predictive of contact and still carry no usable force. Evaluation in this line is detection rate, latency and false positives on a held-out session, which scores the detector while the force it commands can stay wrong. The substrate matured alongside the policies: gel-sensor hardware [ 37 ] , simulators [ 71 , 77 ] , visuo-tactile pretraining [ 20 ] , sim-to-real transfer [ 74 ] and a recent survey [ 80 ] . 2.4 Proxy-Based Evaluation Reporting conventions here are inherited from benchmark suites that score task success alone, or at most one scalar force reading beside it [ 42 , 50 , 30 , 47 , 91 , 12 , 58 , 34 , 79 , 22 , 15 , 14 ] . Adapter and parameter-efficient practice keeps the same convention: the reported columns are loss and success, and the controlled physical quantity is not among them [ 26 , 13 , 25 ] . Contact-aware instrumentation measures the sensor rather than the policy’s outcome [ 37 , 71 , 77 , 20 , 74 ] .
